We need to explain the problem, the assumptions, the reasoning, and why switching yields 2/3 probability. Provide clear examples, perhaps with probability trees, simulation, intuitive explanation, and maybe a formal proof. Also note that the standard Monty Hall problem assumes the host always opens a door that does not contain the car and that the host knows which door has the car and will always open a goat door. Also note that the player initially picks a door at random (1/3 chance of car). Then host opens one of the other two doors, revealing a goat. Then the player can switch to the remaining unopened door. The probability that the car is behind the initially chosen door remains 1/3, so the probability it's behind the other unopened door is 2/3. So switching yields 2/3.

We can also discuss alternative interpretations (if host doesn't always open a goat door, etc). Provide a simple simulation in Python maybe. Provide intuitive explanation: think of 100 doors, host opens 98 goats, etc. Provide the probability tree.
